Skepticism in philosophy is the position that knowledge, or at least certainty, cannot be reliably attained, and that rational suspension of judgment is the wisest response to dogmatic claims. Emerging from Pyrrho of Elis in the fourth century before Christ, skepticism does not claim that nothing can be known dogmatically, but rather argues that for every plausible argument, an equally plausible counter-argument exists. Rather than leading to paralysis, ancient skeptics sought ataraxia, a state of tranquility, by abandoning the fruitless quest for absolute certainty and accepting practical guidance from custom and appearance. This tradition shaped medieval and modern epistemology, from Montaigne through Hume to contemporary discussions of justification and belief.

Skepticism emerged from ancient sources with distinctive figures. Pyrrho of Elis, living around three hundred sixty-five to two hundred seventy-five before Christ, taught that suspension of judgment is the path to tranquility; he traveled with Alexander the Great and incorporated non-Western philosophies. Carneades, from around two hundred fourteen to one hundred twenty-nine before Christ, was head of the Academy and developed systematic skeptical arguments against Stoic epistemology and theory of perception. Importantly, skeptics did not claim that nothing is knowable—a dogmatic assertion—but argued instead that certainty is unattainable and that dogmatism is self-defeating.

The core doctrines rest on equipollence, also called isostheneia: for any convincing argument, an equally convincing counter-argument can be posed. Skeptics practice epoché, suspension of judgment, which is a refusal to assent to dogmatic claims and a practical stance rather than paralysis. The goal is ataraxia, mental tranquility achieved by abandoning the futile pursuit of absolute certainty.

Modern skeptical thought continued this tradition through new figures. Montaigne in the sixteenth century revived Pyrrho and used skepticism to critique dogmatism and pride in human reason. Hume in the eighteenth century argued that causation, induction, and the self are empirically unwarranted, anticipating modern epistemology. Contemporary skepticism about knowledge, justification, and the external world remains central to epistemology. Skepticism addresses a fundamental tension: we crave certainty and systematic knowledge, yet every systematic claim faces objections, yet rather than despair, ancient skepticism was therapeutic, promising liberation from anxiety about ever-failing certainty.
